disclaimer: A score is an evidence-based judgment, not a verdict. It is an estimate from the evidence found, never proof of intent.

factors.label: Sourcing
factors.description: Anonymous or circular sources, no primary document, single-source claim.

factors.label: Verifiability
factors.description: Can the core fact be independently confirmed? Does a second independent source confirm it?

factors.label: Framing and language
factors.description: Loaded words, headline that contradicts the body, emotional trigger words.

factors.label: Omission and context
factors.description: Key facts, dates, denominators or counter-claims left out; old material presented as new.

factors.label: Emotional manipulation
factors.description: Fear, outrage or tribal-identity hooks doing more work than facts.

factors.label: Amplification pattern
factors.description: Identical wording across outlets or accounts, sudden coordinated push, timing that serves an obvious beneficiary.

factors.label: Source incentive
factors.description: Who gains if you believe this, and is that party the source?

method_note: One event per week: the top story with the highest psyop score. In this first build each seeded week was chosen by headline-level screening of that week's top stories, then scored on the seven factors against sources I opened. The score applies to the claim named in 'scored claim', not to the outlets' accurate reporting of it. Unsourced stories are not scored. Weeks marked 'not yet scanned' have no data.

weeks.headline: Judge blocks Trump's White House media ban, orders access to be restored
weeks.scored_claim: The administration's stated rationale that banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House protects national security.
weeks.selection_reason: A court record documents the gap between the stated rationale and the evidence. Chosen at headline level; the other stories screened were not fully scored.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The security claim rested on Justice Department letters sent on Tuesday 9/22, after the ban and after the lawsuit (Reuters), and on Defense Department declarations. The judge said those officials had 'no direct knowledge of how reporters operate in the White House' (BBC).

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: Judge Kelly: 'The record lacks factual support for defendants' contention that the revocation of plaintiffs' hard passes will in fact protect national security' (TRO, quoted by Reuters and BBC).

framing.label: documented
framing.note: The letters cited reporting that 'threatened national security and/or spread falsehoods', blending a security claim with a content complaint (TRO). Trump's post said the outlets 'shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES' (Reuters). The judge said the stories cited 'are routine' (NBC).

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The administration named the specific articles it objected to, so they were not hidden. It left out context that NBC supplies: AP and CNBC ran the same background-briefing story under the same attribution and were not banned. Trump's 9/18 announcement did not mention security (TRO).

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Tribal and fear hooks: 'FAKE NEWS' and 'FICTION and LIES' in Trump's posts (NBC, Reuters), and a security label that implies danger without evidence.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: The security rationale first appeared in the post-suit letters and court filings of 9/22 (Reuters, BBC). It was repeated in later social media posts (court opinion of 10/13, hindsight).

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is speculation
incentive.note: The source is the government, which gains in court from a security label: the TRO notes that review of the executive's national-security determinations is 'highly deferential'. Motive is an inference.

target_audience.text: Federal courts, which defer more to national-security claims, and a public and base receptive to the 'fake news' framing.

confidence.reason: I read the 9/24 TRO and the 10/13 preliminary-injunction opinion directly, and Reuters, BBC and NBC agree. The judge's findings are preliminary ('likely to succeed') and the government disputes them.

weeks.mechanism: Documented: the security rationale appears only after the ban and the lawsuit. The 9/18 announcement cited 'fake news', and the TRO found the record lacked factual support that the ban protects national security. The court later called it 'merely a post-hoc justification'.
weeks.summary: Trump announced on 9/18 that he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, citing 'fake news'. After the outlets sued, the government defended the ban as protecting national security. On 9/24 Judge Kelly ordered access restored for 14 days and found no factual support for the security claim. Reuters, BBC and NBC reported this accurately; the score applies to the claim, not to their reporting.
weeks.counter_argument: The judge called national security a 'weighty' interest and wrote that his ruling should not be read to suggest Trump's concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media's reporting are 'unfounded'. NBC notes some cited articles concerned munitions stockpiles. The findings are preliminary and the government disputes them.
weeks.hindsight_note: After the window (documented, not knowable on 9/24): on 10/13 Judge Kelly granted a preliminary injunction (Doc. 50), finding the outlets likely to succeed on due process and two First Amendment claims. He wrote that 'national security' appears to have been 'merely a post-hoc justification for the decision'.
gaps: Trump's 9/18 Truth Social post and the Justice Department's 9/22 letters were not opened directly. They are quoted from the TRO, Reuters and NBC.

The TRO text was read from a third-party mirror (brynodc.com) of court document 24 in case 1:26-cv-03287-TJK, not from the court's own system. The caption, docket number and 09/24/26 filing date match the 10/13 opinion's description.
The AP original was blocked and the Reuters original is paywalled. Reuters text was read through Yahoo News.
Other top stories of the week were screened at headline level only, not fully scored.

weeks.headline: Trump administration lowers fuel economy standards, critics say at a significant environmental cost
weeks.scored_claim: DOT's and the White House's framing of the 9/28 fuel-economy rollback as ending an 'illegal mandate' and making cars $1,300 cheaper.
weeks.selection_reason: The administration's affordability claim is contested by the agency's own cost analysis, and the 'mandate' wording is called false by AP. Chosen at headline level; the other stories screened were not fully scored.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The headline savings ($1,300 lower average new-vehicle price; $138 billion in consumer savings over five years) come from DOT itself (AP, Roll Call, USA Today). The 892-page final rule is the primary document, but I could not open it.

verifiability.label: disputed
verifiability.note: NHTSA's own regulatory analysis shows drivers spending about $1,624 more on fuel over a vehicle's life (USA Today). The Environmental Defense Fund cites about $1,600 more (Roll Call). The sticker-price estimate is not independently confirmed.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: DOT titled the rule 'Freedom Means Affordable Cars' and Secretary Duffy called it ending an 'illegal mandate'. AP notes that Trump 'falsely calls' it an EV 'mandate' and that no federal policy has mandated EV sales. Trump's preview post called past cars 'Environmental Monsters' (Roll Call).

omission.label: documented
omission.note: DOT's headline figures leave out the roughly $1,624 lifetime fuel-cost increase in NHTSA's own analysis (USA Today). DOT's oil-use comparison is against 2024, while AP notes the prior standards were estimated to save 14 billion gallons of gasoline by 2050.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Appeals to family affordability ('American dream') alongside the 'Environmental Monsters' jab: a mild identity hook. Facts still do most of the work.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: Trump previewed the rule on Truth Social on Saturday 9/26 and DOT released it on Monday 9/28, an ordinary rollout. Automaker statements echo 'market realities' (AP, USA Today), but I found no coordinated push.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is speculation
incentive.note: The agency announcing the savings wrote the rule. Automakers that gain flexibility (the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, Ford, GM, Stellantis) praised it (AP). AP puts it against gas at $4.47 a gallon and the midterms. Motive is an inference.

target_audience.text: Car buyers and households worried about vehicle prices and the cost of living, plus the administration's base and automakers.

confidence.reason: AP, Roll Call, USA Today and Carbon Brief agree on the figures. I could not open the DOT press release or the NHTSA analysis (blocked), so the numbers are read through outlets that quote them.

weeks.summary: On Monday 9/28 DOT released a final rule resetting CAFE standards to about 34.9 mpg for model year 2031, down from the 50.4 mpg projected under the Biden-era rule. It said the change would cut the average new-vehicle price by $1,300. NHTSA's own analysis shows drivers paying about $1,624 more for fuel. The outlets reported both. The score applies to the administration's framing, not to the outlets' reporting.
weeks.counter_argument: DOT did publish the fuel-cost increase in its regulatory analysis, so the figure was disclosed rather than hidden. Whether regulation or the market should set fuel-economy targets is a legitimate policy dispute, and automakers publicly backed the change.
weeks.hindsight_note: This window is under three weeks old. I verified no later outcome yet (AP reports the Sierra Club 'vowed to fight the rule').
gaps: The DOT press release and the NHTSA regulatory analysis were not opened (HTTP 403 to automated access). Figures come from AP, Roll Call and USA Today, which quote them.
The AP original was blocked and the Reuters article is paywalled. AP text was read through PBS News.
The Washington Post's view that analysts 'doubt' the price cut is known only secondhand through Carbon Brief.
Other top stories of the week were screened at headline level only, not fully scored.

weeks.headline: Trump says Russia, Ukraine agree to 'energy ceasefire'
weeks.scored_claim: Trump's claim, posted on Truth Social on 10/11, that Russia and Ukraine 'both agreed' to an immediate energy ceasefire.
weeks.selection_reason: Single-source claim of fact that the named parties did not confirm, with an identifiable source incentive. Chosen at headline level; the other stories screened were not fully scored.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The only source for 'Both parties have agreed' is Trump's own Truth Social post. No document, terms, scope or start time were published. DW and NBC both report no immediate confirmation from Moscow.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: Zelenskyy told Axios within minutes it was 'news for me' (DW). The Kremlin said only that 'contacts are ongoing' (NBC). No second independent source confirmed that an agreement existed.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'Effective immediately... Do not break it!' reads as settled fact plus an enforcement order, while the outlets mostly attributed it ('Trump says', 'Trump claims').

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The post gives no definition of 'energy infrastructure' and no terms for either side. It also leaves out context that NBC and DW report: it followed the 10/09 diesel deal, it came weeks before the 11/03 midterms, and NBC notes a similar announcement a month earlier that neither side confirmed.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: The post is terse. Apart from the imperative 'Do not break it!' it carries no fear or outrage hook.

amplification.label: disputed
amplification.note: The announcement came a day after Trump called for Ukraine to 'get a new leader' (NBC) and two days after the diesel deal. The quote was reproduced identically across outlets, which is normal for a presidential post. I found no evidence of a coordinated account push.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is speculation
incentive.note: The source is also the party that benefits. DW and NBC report that Trump needs lower fuel prices before the midterms and has blamed Ukraine's refinery strikes, not the Iran war, for high diesel prices. A truce halting those strikes would serve that goal. Motive is an inference.

target_audience.text: U.S. voters worried about fuel prices ahead of the 11/03 midterms, and Trump's domestic base. Moscow and Kyiv are secondary audiences, pressured to comply publicly.

confidence.reason: What Trump posted, Zelenskyy's reaction and the lack of confirmation from Moscow are documented by three in-window outlets. I did not open the Truth Social post or the AP and Reuters originals. Motive is inference.

weeks.summary: On Sunday 10/11 Trump posted that an 'ENERGY CEASEFIRE' was in effect and that 'both parties have agreed'. Ukraine's president said it was news to him. Moscow did not confirm. No terms were published. Coverage in the window was accurate and attributed; the score applies to the claim, not to the outlets' reporting.
weeks.counter_argument: Zelenskyy had himself offered on ABC's 'This Week' the same day to stop hitting Russian refineries if Russia stopped hitting Ukraine's grid (NBC). Trump's post may have been a public attempt to bring both sides to a deal they were each already signalling. An unconfirmed announcement is not proof of deception.
weeks.hindsight_note: After the window closed (documented, not knowable on 10/11): Ukrainian officials said Russia kept striking energy sites in the hours after the post and on Monday morning, including near Kharkiv (NBC; Reuters text via The Business Standard). The Kremlin said 'contacts are ongoing' and rejected a 60-day truce (Reuters via The Business Standard; BBC). On 10/12 Trump said 'They agreed because I said they agreed' (RFE/RL). By 10/13 RFE/RL reported that neither side had confirmed the truce.
gaps: The Truth Social post itself was not retrieved. The wording comes from DW, The Guardian and NBC, which quote it identically.

The AP and Reuters originals could not be opened (AP blocks automated access; Reuters is paywalled). Wire content was checked through DW (credits AFP and Reuters) and The Business Standard (Reuters text).
The Axios interview with Zelenskyy was not opened (blocked). The quote is taken from DW, NBC and The Guardian.
No Kremlin primary transcript was opened. Peskov's statements are known only through NBC, BBC and Reuters.
Other top stories of the week were screened at headline level only, not fully scored.
